name: Crockett Lake
terrain: Road shoulders and pullouts along SR 20; a scope does the walking.
when: July through September for shorebirds; winter for raptors. Pair it with the Coupeville ferry and Fort Casey.
access: Free pullouts. Discover Pass if you park at Fort Casey next door.
blurb: A shallow lagoon beside the Coupeville ferry landing that is, acre for acre, the best shorebird spot on this list. Pull off the highway, set up a scope, and let the birds come to you: sandpipers and plovers on the flats, falcons and harriers never far behind.

seasons.note: Northbound shorebirds pass through fast.
Fall shorebird migration starts by early July.
Rarity season; scan every flock.
Raptors work the wet fields at dusk.

name: Juanita Bay Park
terrain: Paved and boardwalk, fully level and stroller-friendly.
when: Any time of day — the boardwalk faces east, so late afternoon light is kindest.
access: Free lot off Market Street. Restrooms on site.
blurb: A short boardwalk out over a cattail marsh, which is a very efficient way to be close to birds without walking far. Beavers, turtles on the logs, and herons standing in the shallows about ten feet from the railing.

seasons.note: Martins take the boxes; osprey rebuild the platform.
Herons fish within feet of the boardwalk rail.
Grebes and mergansers return to the bay.
Goldeneye and wigeon raft off the point.

name: Edmonds Marsh & Waterfront
terrain: Level sidewalk and viewing platforms; the marsh loop is short.
when: High tide pushes birds close on the water; the marsh is good all day.
access: Free. Paid lots near the ferry terminal. Walkable from the Sounder station.
blurb: Two habitats a five-minute walk apart: a saltmarsh with rails and raptors, and a fishing pier that puts you out over the Sound with the scoters and loons. The best cold-weather half-day on this list if you don't want to commit to a hike.

seasons.note: Alcids move north past the pier; the marsh greens up.
Guillemots nest under the ferry dock.
Loons and grebes reappear on the Sound.
The best sea-duck watching in the county.

name: Union Bay Natural Area (Montlake Fill)
terrain: Gravel paths, level the whole way (about 10 ft gain).
when: Early morning, any season. Shorebirding is best in late summer as water levels drop.
access: Free. Street parking or UW lots (fee on weekdays). Reachable by light rail.
blurb: Seattle's most-birded patch: a restored landfill on Lake Washington beside the UW campus with more than 260 species recorded. Ponds, marsh, and meadow packed into a flat, easy loop, and something is always happening — rails muttering in the cattails, eagles working the bay, a steady parade of local birders happy to share what's around.

seasons.note: Marsh fills with song; teal and swallows arrive.
Rails call from the cattails at dawn.
Mudflats emerge — the best shorebirding of the year.
Ponds crowd with wintering ducks and swans.

sources.title: UW Botanic Gardens: Union Bay Natural Area
WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington

name: Magnuson Park
terrain: Paved and packed gravel, gentle grades.
when: Morning. Spring migration is the headline here.
access: Free. Large lots. Frequent bus service.
blurb: A former naval air station now stitched with constructed ponds and thickets, which turns out to be exactly what migrating sparrows and warblers want. Loud with song in May and pleasantly empty on winter mornings.

seasons.note: Peak migration — warblers and tanagers in the thickets.
Martins over the ponds, swallows over the meadow.
Sparrows flood the shrub-steppe plantings.
Open grass draws shrikes and hunting raptors.

name: Seward Park
terrain: Paved perimeter loop, level; forest trails climb modestly.
when: Dawn for the forest birds; the loop is busy with joggers by nine.
access: Free lots. Restrooms and a café at the entrance.
blurb: A peninsula of genuine old growth inside city limits — big Douglas-firs, pileateds hammering somewhere above you, and eagles nesting where the trail meets the water. Do the forest first, then walk the shoreline for grebes.

seasons.note: Flycatchers and vireos fill the old growth.
Pileateds work the big snags; osprey overhead.
Thrushes and kinglets drop into the understory.
Owls call before dawn; grebes offshore.

sources.title: Greater Seattle on the Cheap: Bird watching in the Puget Sound region

name: Marymoor Park
terrain: Flat gravel and boardwalk; can be muddy after rain.
when: Very early — this is a busy park. Dawn chorus in June is the reason to come.
blurb: Behind the dog park and the cricket pitch there's a cottonwood bottomland along the Sammamish Slough that produces an outsized species list. The boardwalk to the lake is where most of it happens.

seasons.note: Orioles and buntings in the cottonwood edge.
Dawn chorus in the bottomland is the reason to come.
Sparrows and snipe in the wet meadow.
Meadowlark and shrike out in the open field.

sources.title: WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington

name: Billy Frank Jr. Nisqually NWR
terrain: Level gravel and a mile of boardwalk over the estuary.
when: Time the tide: arrive two hours before high water for the shorebirds.
access: $3 per vehicle (federal passes accepted). Visitor center and restrooms.
blurb: The south Sound's great estuary, and the single most reliable stop on this list. The boardwalk carries you a mile out into the tideflats, which means you're standing in the middle of the birds rather than looking at them across a field.

seasons.note: Western Sandpipers stream through on the tide.
Osprey and terns work the estuary all day.
Dowitchers and dunlin in the thousands.
Geese, swans, and pintail fill the freshwater ponds.

sources.title: USFWS: Billy Frank Jr. Nisqually NWR

name: Discovery Park
terrain: Loop trail rolls; add 1.5 mi round trip and 200 ft of climb for West Point beach.
when: Morning for songbirds, falling tide for the beach.
access: Free. Three lots; the south lot is closest to the bluff.
blurb: Five hundred acres of forest and bluff meadow with the Sound at the bottom of it — the widest habitat range of anywhere on this list. Budget the extra descent to West Point; the lighthouse beach is where the loons and alcids are.

seasons.note: Migrants drop into the forest edges; terns return to the Sound.
Guillemots and auklets fish off West Point; martins use the snags.
Seawatching picks up; sparrows flood the meadows.
The best season at West Point: loons, grebes, and sea ducks close to shore.

name: Fort Ebey State Park
terrain: Forest singletrack and bluff trail with modest ups and downs.
when: Morning in the woods, afternoon seawatch from the bluff.
access: Discover Pass required. Restrooms at the Gun Battery lot.
blurb: A former coastal defense fort where dense woods meet a high bluff over the Strait. Owls and woodpeckers in the trees, and below the bluff a seawatch over kelp beds where scoters, loons, and auklets ride the tide rips. Pairs with Crockett Lake for a full Whidbey day.

seasons.note: Owlets fledge near the gun battery.
Auklets feed in the rips below the bluff.
Seabirds stream past the point.
Quiet trails, busy water.

sources.title: WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington

name: Spencer Island
habitat: Dike loop, freshwater and tidal marsh
terrain: Flat, exposed grass-and-gravel dike; 6.6 mi round trip from the lot via the Langus riverfront trail and the 1914 Jackknife Bridge. No shade, no water.
when: Fall and winter. Bring a scope and something windproof.
access: Free gravel lot at Langus Riverfront Park; walk in along the river. No dogs on the south (county) half.
blurb: A working estuary in the Snohomish delta: dikes, sloughs, and a lot of sky. Raptor density in winter is the best in the county — harriers low over the grass, eagles by the dozen, and a decent chance at a shrike.

seasons.note: Bitterns boom from the sloughs; teal pair off.
Rails and wrens everywhere in the tidal marsh.
Snipe and yellowlegs work the drawdown.
Raptor density peaks — harriers, rough-legs, shrikes.

name: Ebey's Landing
terrain: Steady 260 ft climb to the bluff, then loose cobble on the beach return.
when: Clear days for the raptor watch. Spring for the prairie.
access: Free lot at the Prairie Overlook; the beach lot needs a Discover Pass. Ferry from Mukilteo.
blurb: One of the best walks in the state that also happens to be excellent birding: historic prairie on the bluff top, the Strait wide open below, and a return along the beach past Perego's Lagoon. Come for the view and get the birds as a bonus.

seasons.note: Prairie birds return to the bluff top.
Alcids below the bluff; vultures riding the updraft.
Falcon migration along the ridge line.
Short-eared owls hunt the prairie at dusk.

sources.title: NPS: Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve

name: Dungeness Spit
terrain: Half a mile of forest down to the beach, then five miles of soft sand and cobble each way.
when: Falling tide, all day, and start early. Any season rewards it; winter is best for sea ducks.
access: $3 per family/group, daily (federal passes accepted). Dungeness Recreation Area lot. No dogs.
blurb: Five and a half miles of sand thrown out into the Strait of Juan de Fuca — the longest natural sand spit in the country, and a full day's commitment. Harbor on one side, open strait on the other, birds on both, and a lighthouse at the end to justify the walk back.

seasons.note: Brant and whimbrel stage along the spit.
Auklets and guillemots in the strait.
Jaegers and grebes from the outer spit.
Long-tailed and harlequin ducks in the harbor.

sources.title: WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington
